prize_parts.citation: For a visionary prose and poetry in Romanian that turns memory, the body and dream into an inner cosmos of rare formal ambition and imaginative depth.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B050, a single credited name, Mircea Cărtărescu. The case rests on the whole oeuvre and the common criteria, not on the round-1 pattern, which I do not treat as evidence of merit. The chair asked which works each member relies on. I rely on Blinding (the first part of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid for the large-scale prose architecture. For breadth I rely on the poetic origin and the essays. By public knowledge these are the parts of the corpus I know least well, so the whole-oeuvre claim is partly inferred. What persuades me is the voice, which I recognise in the writing and nowhere else. It is combined with a formal logic, a recurring set of images and a long sentence design that holds a very large construction together. Memory, the body and dream are not decoration but the method of a sustained metaphysical project. On the late-volume question, I read the recurring motifs as the architecture of a personal mythology, which is an interpretation and not a verified finding. If the committee reads the later books and concludes that they only enlarge the machinery, I would weaken my view. A single-writer citation raises no attribution problem and needs no regional or political support. On the chair's last question, I see no merit or citation reason to prefer no award (P000) this year. My reservations are about evidence and are not strong enough to justify withholding the prize. I order my alternatives B009 then B001. This reflects the weight of the arguments in round 1 and not a change of first choice. Olsson's strict framing of Zurita's citation around the written sequences answers the scope problem I had. Four colleagues' doubts about NDiaye's breadth are ones I cannot answer with close reading.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged, and no round-1 file resolved it: whether the late, very large volumes deepen the project or repeat its motifs. All six files raised it and none offers verified close-reading evidence, mine included. A second reservation is that the Romanian prose reaches us through translation, which may only partly carry the rhythm, syntax and long architecture on which the effect depends. The poetry, essays and early work are the least covered part of the corpus for me, so the claim of a whole oeuvre rests more on the major novels than I would like. The chair has also asked for the strongest alternative case to be stated honestly. I cannot show that Cărtărescu's late work is better than Zurita's or NDiaye's controlled shorter forms. My preference is a judgment about scale, voice and imaginative range, and a committee that weights compression and formal economy differently could reasonably reach another view.

responses.point: Olsson moved Cărtărescu to first place from his opening Zurita ranking and keeps B009 as his first alternative. He says his reservations about Zurita concern translation loss, dependence on non-textual interventions and reliance on a single sequential project. He also accepts that any citation would have to be worded strictly around the written poems.
responses.response: I agree with the strict scope, and it is the main reason I can keep Zurita as a serious alternative. A citation naming Purgatory and Anteparadise as written poetry would answer my earlier worry that the landscape work would carry credit that belongs to literature. I differ on the remaining point. You say Cărtărescu's recurrence works across prose and poetry while Zurita's depends on a narrower generic range. I see that as a real difference of scope, but I do not treat it as a decisive merit advantage, because a sustained single-genre project can be a strong achievement. I would put the decisive question to the committee in your terms: do the written sequences stand as poems in Spanish, apart from their historical occasion? I cannot answer that from translation. If readers of the Spanish said yes, I would give B009 more weight than my round-1 ranking did.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg keeps B050 first on the common criteria but says the late volumes may be self-enclosed or repetitive, and that the committee should test this directly. He names Zurita (B009) and Yan Lianke (B024) as alternatives, and argues that Yan's mythorealism is a formal contribution, not testimony.
responses.response: I agree that the committee should test the repetition question rather than assume the answer, and I would say that applies to my own reading of recurrence as personal mythology. A useful test would be whether later volumes alter the project, through changed structure, new registers or a different relation between the personal and the historical. If they only re-enter the same images, your worry stands. On Yan Lianke, I accept that the poetics is a literary strategy and I would not rest anything on censorship. I still hold that I cannot judge uneven quality across a large corpus through translation. I would not move him into my alternatives unless readers of the Chinese could say that the strongest books carry the oeuvre.

responses.point: Carlberg ranked NDiaye fourth. She admires the control of her voice, but doubts that the whole body of work matches the imaginative range and structural ambition of the strongest candidates, and says she would revisit this if colleagues who know the plays and later novels argued that they deepen the early fiction.
responses.response: That invitation, which the chair repeats, deserves a direct answer. As I understand the public record, the main claim rests on the shorter and middle-length fiction named in the entry, Three Strong Women and My Heart Hemmed In, together with the novels around them and the theatre. What I value there is a repeated formal problem: an uncanny, precisely controlled voice used on exclusion, inherited family power and unstable belonging, and it changes in how it is posed from book to book. I cannot demonstrate that development as close reading, and I know the plays less well than the fiction. I accept your point that her oeuvre is more compact and less architecturally ambitious than Cărtărescu's. That is why NDiaye stays an alternative, now second, and not my first choice. I would still resist treating compactness alone as a limit on significance.

responses.point: Sward keeps Cărtărescu first, names Tawada (B018) and Zurita (B009) as alternatives, and now accepts that Zurita deserves more weight than her opening ranking gave him. She says the repetition worry argues for judging the cycles as a whole and not the late volumes alone. She also says Tawada's shorter, fragmentary forms are harder to weigh against epic-scale bodies of work.
responses.response: I agree that the cycles should be judged as wholes, and it also answers part of the chair's question about which works to rely on: the argument has to be made on the trilogy and Solenoid together, not on whichever volume a reader met first. On Tawada, my round-1 answer was that I did not rank her and know her work less well. That remains true, and I do not want to rank her above candidates I know better. Your question about whether short forms sustain depth is fair. The Japanese and German bodies of work need readers of both languages, and I cannot supply that. I note that your move on Zurita and mine point to the same condition: the committee should say which texts it relies on and who can read them in the original.

uncertainties: How much of the syntax, rhythm and long sentence architecture of Cărtărescu's Romanian survives in the translations the committee uses, and how fairly those translations represent the poetry, essays and early prose.
Whether the late volumes deepen the project or only enlarge it. This is the one question all six round-1 files left open, and I cannot settle it without close reading of the whole corpus.
Whether Zurita's written sequences carry the case on their own in Spanish, apart from the landscape-scale and memorial work, and how a citation limited to the poems would be worded and judged.
Whether NDiaye's compact oeuvre, including the plays, which I know less well and which are less widely translated, has the cumulative weight of a whole-authorship prize.

Corpus-coverage gaps for Tawada, Yan Lianke, Adonis, Michon and Couto: my knowledge rests on public knowledge of representative works, and the committee's ability to read the originals is not established.

All judgments rest on public knowledge of the works. I have not read texts in this session or independently verified any source. This is a modelled committee recommendation and not the decision of the full Swedish Academy.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. None apparent from the supplied profile, which lists no personal, institutional or translation connection to any shortlisted writer. My practice as a historical and psychological novelist and critic is context, not evidence of preference. I have kept my position because of the common criteria and not because of the round-1 pattern, and I record that my alternatives are reordered, with first choice unchanged. No recusal is proposed.
